title: Lipid Synthesis: Building Cholesterol from Acetyl-CoA

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What are the two ways a liver cell gets cholesterol?
cards.back: It makes it from acetyl-CoA, or it imports it as LDL through the LDL receptor.
cards.quote: A liver cell gets cholesterol two ways: it makes it from acetyl-CoA, or it imports it as LDL through the LDL receptor.

cards.front: What single gauge sets both cholesterol supply lines in a liver cell, and what does a low reading do?
cards.back: The cholesterol level in the ER membrane. When it reads low, the cell turns up both the synthesis genes (led by HMG-CoA reductase) and the LDL-receptor gene; high turns both down.
cards.quote: Both supply lines run off one gauge, the cholesterol level in the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).

cards.front: Brown and Goldstein gave radioactive-iodine-labeled LDL to skin cells from normal people and from children with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). What did they see, and what did it show?
cards.back: Normal cells took up a lot of LDL; FH cells barely took any. FH is a disorder of LDL uptake, not of synthesis.
cards.quote: Brown and Goldstein tagged LDL with radioactive iodine and measured how much each kind of cell took in.

cards.front: All 27 of cholesterol's carbons come from {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}, across roughly thirty enzymatic steps.
cards.quote: All 27 of cholesterol's carbons come from acetyl-CoA, across roughly thirty enzymatic steps

cards.front: What reaction does HMG-CoA reductase catalyze, with what cofactor, and where does the enzyme sit?
cards.back: HMG-CoA to mevalonate, using two NADPH. It sits in the ER membrane with its working end facing the cytosol.
cards.why: It runs the main rate-limiting, irreversible step of cholesterol synthesis.
cards.quote: Then HMG-CoA reductase uses two NADPH to make mevalonate.

cards.front: Starting from the C5 unit isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and its isomer DMAPP, what are the C10 and C15 products of head-to-tail coupling?
cards.back: Geranyl-PP (C10), then farnesyl-PP (C15). Each coupling releases pyrophosphate.
cards.quote: C5 plus C5 gives geranyl-PP (C10), and one more C5 gives farnesyl-PP (C15).

cards.front: In cholesterol synthesis, what pulls the prenyl coupling reactions forward?
cards.back: Hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate each coupling releases.
cards.quote: Hydrolysis of the released pyrophosphate pulls each coupling forward.

cards.front: Eighteen acetyl-CoA make one cholesterol. Account for the carbons from 36 brought in to 27 in cholesterol.
cards.back: 18 x 2 = 36 C. Each of six mevalonates loses one CO₂ becoming IPP: 6 x 5 = 30 C in squalene and lanosterol. Trimming removes three methyls: 30 - 3 = 27.
cards.quote: Six leave as CO₂, one from each mevalonate as it becomes IPP, so six IPP carry 30 carbons.

cards.front: How many ATP and NADPH does it cost to go from acetyl-CoA to 2,3-oxidosqualene, the epoxide before cyclization?
cards.back: ATP: 6 IPP x 3 = 18. NADPH: 6 reductase turns x 2 = 12, plus 1 at squalene synthase and 1 at squalene monooxygenase = 14. More NADPH is spent in the trimming.
cards.quote: So making one cholesterol costs 18 acetyl-CoA, 18 ATP and 14 NADPH (12 + 1 + 1) just to reach the epoxide

cards.front: Using the cholesterol pathway's ledger, how many acetyl-CoA, ATP and NADPH go into one farnesyl-PP (C15), and how many carbons are lost as CO₂?
cards.back: Farnesyl-PP = 3 IPP. Each IPP needs 1 mevalonate (3 acetyl-CoA, 2 NADPH, 3 ATP). So 9 acetyl-CoA (18 C), 6 NADPH, 9 ATP; 3 CO₂ lost, leaving 15 C.
cards.quote: Three ATP phosphorylate mevalonate, and it loses one CO₂ to become isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), the universal five-carbon unit.

cards.front: Why does it make sense for the main brake on cholesterol synthesis to be HMG-CoA reductase rather than a later step?
cards.back: Braking at the reductase stops carbon before any ATP is spent on the phosphorylation steps that follow.
cards.quote: The cell puts its main brake at the reductase, so it stops carbon before any ATP is spent on the phosphorylation steps.

cards.front: In the mevalonate pathway, what does HMG-CoA reductase commit carbon to, and what does squalene synthase commit it to?
cards.back: The reductase commits carbon to the mevalonate trunk, which still branches; squalene synthase commits it to sterols alone.
cards.quote: the reductase commits carbon to the mevalonate trunk (which still branches), and squalene synthase commits it to sterols alone.

cards.front: Besides cholesterol, what products are built from mevalonate's C5 units?
cards.back: CoQ10, dolichol, the side chain of one form of vitamin K, and the prenyl anchors (farnesyl-PP, geranylgeranyl-PP) that tether proteins such as Ras.
cards.quote: Its C5 units also feed CoQ10, dolichol, the side chain of one form of vitamin K, and the prenyl anchors

cards.front: Drug A is a statin; compound B blocks squalene synthase. Which one is more likely to reduce farnesyl-PP anchoring of Ras to membranes, and why?
cards.back: The statin. Farnesyl-PP lies on the shared trunk above squalene synthase, so blocking squalene synthase spares it, while a statin cuts the whole isoprenoid supply.
cards.quote: A statin acts at the top of the trunk and cuts the whole isoprenoid supply, CoQ10 and the prenyl anchors included.

cards.front: {{c1::ApoB-100}} is the address label the LDL receptor reads.
cards.quote: ApoB-100 is the address label the LDL receptor reads.

cards.front: Why does cholesterol travel in lipoproteins, and how is a lipoprotein arranged?
cards.back: Cholesterol does not dissolve in blood. A lipoprotein has a shell of phospholipid, free cholesterol and apolipoprotein around a core of triacylglycerol and cholesteryl ester.
cards.quote: a shell of phospholipid, free cholesterol and apolipoprotein around a core of triacylglycerol and cholesteryl ester

cards.front: After LDL binds its receptor and enters by receptor-mediated endocytosis, what happens to the receptor and to the LDL?
cards.back: The receptors cluster in a clathrin-coated pit that pinches off. In the acidic endosome LDL lets go; the receptor recycles to the surface, and LDL goes to the lysosome, which releases free cholesterol.
cards.quote: The receptor recycles to the cell surface, while the LDL goes on to the lysosome, which breaks it down and releases free cholesterol.

cards.front: A mutant LDL receptor binds ApoB-100 normally but never gathers into clathrin-coated pits. Predict the effect on LDL uptake and blood LDL.
cards.back: Uptake fails and LDL stays in the blood, as in familial hypercholesterolemia.
cards.why: Uptake needs both binding and clustering into a pit that pinches off as a vesicle; binding alone is not enough.
cards.quote: Even a receptor that binds LDL fails if it never gathers into a pit

cards.front: What usually causes familial hypercholesterolemia, and about how common is it?
cards.back: An inherited LDL-receptor mutation; roughly one person in 250.
cards.quote: an inherited disorder usually caused by an LDL-receptor mutation, found in roughly one person in 250

cards.front: Name the three parts of the ER sterol gauge and the role of each.
cards.back: SREBP-2: the passenger, an inactive transcription factor in the ER membrane. SCAP: its escort, whose sterol-sensing domain reads cholesterol. Insig: grabs SCAP once SCAP has bound cholesterol.
cards.quote: SCAP is its escort, and SCAP's sterol-sensing domain is what actually reads cholesterol.

cards.front: When ER cholesterol is low, what steps take SREBP-2 from the ER membrane to the nucleus?
cards.back: SCAP escorts SREBP-2 in COPII vesicles to the Golgi; S1P and then S2P cut it; the freed piece enters the nucleus and binds the sterol regulatory element.
cards.quote: is cut twice in the Golgi, first by the protease S1P and then by S2P; the freed piece enters the nucleus and binds the sterol regulatory element

cards.front: A cell carries a SCAP mutant whose sterol-sensing domain cannot bind cholesterol. Cholesterol in its ER is high. Predict SREBP-2 processing and LDL-receptor expression.
cards.back: SREBP-2 keeps being processed, so synthesis genes and the LDL receptor stay on despite high cholesterol.
cards.why: Insig grabs SCAP only after SCAP binds cholesterol; without binding, SCAP is not held in the ER and keeps carrying SREBP-2 to the Golgi.
cards.quote: Insig is an ER membrane protein that grabs SCAP once SCAP has bound cholesterol.

cards.front: Of the four controls on HMG-CoA reductase (transcription, degradation, translation, phosphorylation), which one reads something other than the pathway's products, and what does it read?
cards.back: Phosphorylation by AMPK. It reads the cell's energy charge and switches the enzyme off within minutes when ATP is low.
cards.quote: Three of the four read the pathway's own products; only AMPK reads fuel, a famine brake on an expensive molecule.

cards.front: Which of the four controls on HMG-CoA reductase also sets LDL-receptor numbers, and on what time scale does it act?
cards.back: Transcription through SREBP-2, the gauge itself. It works over hours, because it changes how much protein is made.
cards.quote: Of the four, only the transcription control, the gauge itself, also sets the LDL receptor.

cards.front: ATP falls in a liver cell and AMPK is activated. Predict the fast effect on HMG-CoA reductase activity, and whether AMPK itself raises LDL receptors.
cards.back: The reductase is switched off by phosphorylation within minutes. AMPK does not directly raise LDL receptors, because it acts on the enzyme, not through the sterol gauge.
cards.why: Only the SREBP transcription control sets the LDL receptor.
cards.quote: AMPK (last row of the table) also switches off fatty-acid synthesis, and it acts mainly on the enzyme itself, not through the sterol gauge.

cards.front: A statin blocks HMG-CoA reductase in the liver. Predict the change in hepatic LDL receptors and in blood LDL, and explain.
cards.back: Receptors go up and blood LDL goes down. Less synthesis lowers ER cholesterol, the gauge reads low, and SREBP-2 turns on the LDL-receptor gene.
cards.why: The drug works largely by boosting uptake; statins lower blood LDL on average by 30 to 50 percent.
cards.quote: The statin closes one supply line and the gauge opens the other, so a drug that blocks synthesis ends up working largely by boosting uptake.

cards.front: A liver cell is treated with a statin. What happens to the amount of HMG-CoA reductase protein, and why?
cards.back: It rises. The low ER cholesterol reading also turns up the reductase gene, so the cell makes extra enzyme for the drug to block.
cards.quote: The low reading also turns the reductase gene up, so a treated cell makes extra reductase for the drug to block.

cards.front: Skin cells from a child with no working LDL receptors are grown with LDL in the medium. Do they make more or less cholesterol than normal cells, and why?
cards.back: More. No LDL gets in, so the gauge reads low however much LDL is outside, and SREBP-2 keeps synthesis running.
cards.why: The cell reads cholesterol that reaches its interior, not the cholesterol around it.
cards.quote: No LDL gets in, so the cell's gauge reads low however much LDL is in the medium, and SREBP-2 keeps synthesis running.

cards.front: In a child with familial hypercholesterolemia, why is blood LDL high in the whole body?
cards.back: Mainly because LDL is cleared slowly, not because her liver makes much more cholesterol; the liver still gets cholesterol by other routes.
cards.quote: her blood LDL is high mainly because LDL is cleared slowly, not because her liver makes much more

cards.front: A patient's LDL is 200 mg/dL. A statin lowers it by 40 percent; a PCSK9 antibody is then added and lowers the remaining LDL by about 55 percent. Estimate the final LDL, assuming the effects multiply.
cards.back: 200 x 0.60 = 120 mg/dL on the statin; 120 x 0.45 = 54 mg/dL with the antibody added.
cards.quote: PCSK9 antibodies lower LDL by about 55 percent, alone or on top of a statin

cards.front: Why does a statin give back part of its LDL-lowering gain?
cards.back: SREBP-2 also turns on PCSK9, a secreted protein that binds the LDL receptor and sends it to the lysosome, so fewer receptors return to the surface.
cards.quote: SREBP-2 also turns on the gene for PCSK9, a secreted protein that binds the LDL receptor and sends it to the lysosome to be destroyed

cards.front: A patient already on a statin adds an antibody that blocks PCSK9. Predict the change in hepatic LDL receptors and blood LDL.
cards.back: Receptors rise further and LDL falls further, because more of the receptors the statin ordered survive instead of being destroyed.
cards.quote: With PCSK9 blocked, more of the receptors the statin ordered survive.

cards.front: A bile-acid resin traps bile acids in the gut. Predict the effect on liver-cell ER cholesterol and on LDL receptors.
cards.back: ER cholesterol falls, because the liver converts more of its own cholesterol into new bile acids; the gauge reads low and makes more LDL receptors.
cards.quote: Bile-acid resins trap bile acids in the gut, so the liver converts more of its own cholesterol into new bile acids.

cards.front: A patient takes ezetimibe, which blocks cholesterol absorption. Predict what happens in liver cells to LDL-receptor expression and to HMG-CoA reductase expression.
cards.back: Both rise. Less cholesterol reaches the liver from the gut, ER cholesterol falls, and SREBP-2 turns on both the LDL-receptor gene and the synthesis genes.
cards.why: One gauge sets both supply lines; the rise in synthesis is the same compensation a statin triggers.
cards.quote: Ezetimibe blocks cholesterol absorption, so less cholesterol reaches the liver from the gut.

cards.front: A patient with familial hypercholesterolemia has no functional LDL receptors (receptor-null). Would a PCSK9 antibody lower her LDL much? Explain.
cards.back: Probably little. PCSK9 acts by destroying LDL receptors, so with none working there is almost nothing for the antibody to save (inferred from the lesson, which states this only for statins).
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the gauge's LDL-lowering step needs working receptors.
cards.quote: Without them, as in the FH child, the gauge calls for receptors that cannot be added, so a statin loses most of its LDL-lowering step.

cards.front: {{c1::CYP7A1}}, the 7alpha-hydroxylase, commits cholesterol to bile salts.
cards.quote: CYP7A1, the 7alpha-hydroxylase, commits cholesterol to bile salts.

cards.front: From what precursor and where is vitamin D made, and where is it activated?
cards.back: From 7-dehydrocholesterol, a late precursor of cholesterol, in skin; then activated in liver and kidney.
cards.quote: Vitamin D, a secosteroid hormone made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol, a late precursor of cholesterol, then activated in liver and kidney.

cards.front: A patient takes an aromatase inhibitor. Which class of steroid product falls, and which enzyme is blocked?
cards.back: Estrogens fall, because the P450 aromatase that makes them from steroid precursors is blocked.
cards.quote: tailored by tissue-specific enzymes such as the P450 aromatase, which makes estrogens, and 5alpha-reductase

cards.front: How is phosphatidate made from glycerol 3-phosphate?
cards.back: GPAT adds a fatty acid at sn-1, making lysophosphatidate; AGPAT adds the second at sn-2, making phosphatidate.
cards.quote: GPAT adds a fatty acid to glycerol 3-phosphate at the sn-1 position, making lysophosphatidate
cards.section: The other two fates of acetyl-CoA: the phosphatidate hub

cards.front: Phosphatidate is a fork. What are the two ways it is processed, and what does each lead to?
cards.back: Remove the phosphate (PAP, lipins) to diacylglycerol: triacylglycerol, or phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine via CDP-head groups. Add CTP: phosphatidate becomes CDP-diacylglycerol, the donor for phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol, cardiolipin.
cards.quote: Phosphatidate becomes CDP-diacylglycerol, the activated donor for phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin
cards.section: The other two fates of acetyl-CoA: the phosphatidate hub

cards.front: Cultured fat cells are treated with epinephrine. Predict the phosphorylation and location of Lipin 1, and its PAP output.
cards.back: Lipin 1 is dephosphorylated and moves onto the ER membrane, where its substrate phosphatidate lives, so it makes more diacylglycerol.
cards.why: Heavily phosphorylated Lipin 1 stays in the cytosol, away from its substrate, and makes less.
cards.quote: In cultured fat cells, epinephrine and the fatty acid oleate dephosphorylate Lipin 1 and move it onto the membrane
cards.section: Lipin 1 localization in cultured fat cells

cards.front: Prenyl couplings in cholesterol synthesis and CDP-head-group activation in phospholipid synthesis share one thermodynamic trick. What is it?
cards.back: Both release pyrophosphate, and its hydrolysis pulls the reaction forward, the same logic as UDP-sugars.
cards.quote: making the activated head group releases pyrophosphate, whose hydrolysis pulls the reaction forward.
cards.section: The other two fates of acetyl-CoA: the phosphatidate hub

cards.front: An infant lacks hexosaminidase A. What lipid builds up, where, and with what result?
cards.back: The ganglioside GM2 builds up in the lysosomes of neurons, causing fatal neurodegeneration (Tay-Sachs disease).
cards.quote: loss of hexosaminidase A blocks breakdown of the ganglioside GM2, which builds up in the lysosomes of neurons
